lesson.title: Extinction: When the Learned Response Fades
lesson.summary: Extinction is the gradual weakening and eventual disappearance of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus it once predicted.
lesson.body:
Once a response has been acquired, it is not permanent. If the conditioned stimulus keeps showing up without the unconditioned stimulus that originally gave it meaning, the conditioned response gradually weakens and eventually stops appearing at all. This process is extinction, and it makes sense from an adaptive standpoint: if a signal stops predicting anything, an organism that keeps responding to it is wasting effort.

Pavlov demonstrated this with the same dogs from his acquisition studies. After the dogs had learned to salivate at the sound, he began presenting it repeatedly without ever following it with food. At first the dogs still salivated, but with each unrewarded presentation the response grew weaker, until eventually the sound no longer produced any salivation at all.

It is tempting to think of extinction as simply erasing the original learning, but that is not quite accurate, and this is one of the more important nuances in this area of psychology. Extinction is better understood as new learning layered on top of the old association, essentially the organism learning that the conditioned stimulus no longer predicts the unconditioned stimulus, rather than forgetting the original pairing altogether. The evidence for this comes from a phenomenon Pavlov also observed: after an extinguished response had seemingly disappeared, it could reappear on its own after a period of rest, with no additional pairings at all. That reappearance is spontaneous recovery, and it only makes sense if the original association was suppressed rather than deleted.
